title: Senecio inaequidens
wikitext:
{{Short description|Species of flowering plant in the daisy family}} {{Speciesbox |name = |image = Senecio inaequidens 1.jpg |taxon = Senecio inaequidens |authority = [[A. P. de Candolle|DC.]] (1838 ) |synonyms = ''Senecio madagascarensis'', ''Senecio harveianus''
Sources: CABI,{{cite web |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/49557 | access-date = 24 September 2019 | title = Senecio Inaequidens | publisher = CAB International | date = 24 September 2019}} IPNI,{{IPNI | id = 245637-1 | date = 2008-05-25 }} AFPD{{cite web | url = http://www.ville-ge.ch/cjb/bd/africa/details.php?langue=an&id=98173 | title = ''Senecio inaequidens'' DC. record n° 98173 | access-date = 2008-05-25 | work = African Plants Database | publisher = [[Natural History Museum of Geneva|South African National Biodiversity Institute, the Conservatoire et Jardin botaniques de la Ville de Genève]] and Tela Botanica }} |}} '''''Senecio inaequidens''''', known as '''narrow-leaved ragwort'''{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }} and '''South African ragwort''',{{PLANTS|id=SEIN10|taxon=Senecio inaequidens|accessdate=9 November 2015}} is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the daisy family [[Asteraceae]]. ==Description== ''Senecio inaequidens'' is a [[perennial]] [[chamaephyte]] up to {{Convert|1|m|abbr=on}} in height, often much [[Ramification (botany)|ramified]], with each stem ending in one or a few [[pseudanthium|capitula]] yellow in colour, forming a loose floral display. A single plant produces 26 to 500 capitula each year, with approximately 90 florets, 74% of them developing a viable [[Asteraceae#Fruits and seeds|achene]].{{cite journal |last1=Vanparys |first1=Valérie |last2=Cawoy |first2=Valérie |last3=Mahaux |first3=Olivia |last4=Jacquemart |first4=Anne-Laure |title=Comparative study of the reproductive ecology of two co-occurring related plant species: the invasive Senecio inaequidens and the native Jacobaea vulgaris |journal=Plant Ecology and Evolution |date=25 March 2011 |volume=144 |issue=1 |pages=3–11 |doi=10.5091/plecevo.2011.434|doi-access=free }} The leaves are linear, entire or almost so and without petioles. ''S. inaequidens'' exists as a [[diploid]] genotype and a [[tetraploid]] cytotype. Initially the diploid ''S. madagascarensis'' and ''S. harveianus'' were assumed to be different species; however molecular analysis showed that they only differ in [[Karyotype|cytotype]].{{cite journal |last1=Scott |first1=L. J. |last2=Congdon |first2=B. C. |last3=Playford |first3=J. |title=Molecular evidence that fireweed (Senecio madagascariensis, Asteraceae) is of South African origin |journal=Plant Systematics and Evolution |date=1998 |volume=213 |issue=3–4 |pages=251–257 |doi=10.1007/BF00985204|s2cid=39040180 }} ==Distribution== It is native to Southern Africa, including [[Lesotho]], [[South Africa]], [[Eswatini]], [[Namibia]], [[Mozambique]] and [[Botswana]].{{GRIN | accessdate = 2020-04-23 }} ===Habitat=== In its native habitat ''S. inaequidens'' occurs at elevations from sea level to 2,850 m in a wide range of naturally or anthropogenically disturbed habitats such as river banks, rocky slopes, heavily grazed or recently burned grasslands, and road verges.{{cite journal |last1=Lachmuth |first1=Susanne |last2=Durka |first2=Walter |last3=Schurr |first3=Frank M. |title=Differentiation of reproductive and competitive ability in the invaded range of Senecio inaequidens: the role of genetic Allee effects, adaptive and nonadaptive evolution |journal=New Phytologist |date=October 2011 |volume=192 |issue=2 |pages=529–541 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-8137.2011.03808.x|pmid=21736567 |doi-access=free }} The tetraploid [[cytotype]] was only found in the [[Drakensberg|uKhalhamba]] and [[Maloti Mountains|Maloti]] mountain ranges, and this is the cytotype of ''S. inaequidens'' which was inadvertently exported to Europe. [[File:20180726Senecio inaequidens2.jpg|thumb|''S. inaequidens'' is mostly found along railways and motorways.]] ===Invasive spread=== The plant is a widespread [[neophyte (botany)|neophyte]] in [[Europe]] and an [[invasive species]] in Central Europe.{{cite web |title=Senecio inaequidens (South African ragwort) |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/49557#F4A6E092-9C11-43AD-A2E5-4ECEBF33260F |website=www.cabi.org |access-date=24 September 2019 |language=en}} It was introduced through wool imports from Southern Africa. In Europe the ports of entry were Bremen, Calais, Mazamet, and Verviers.{{cite journal |last1=LACHMUTH |first1=SUSANNE |last2=DURKA |first2=WALTER |last3=SCHURR |first3=FRANK M. |title=The making of a rapid plant invader: genetic diversity and differentiation in the native and invaded range of Senecio inaequidens |journal=Molecular Ecology |date=September 2010 |volume=19 |issue=18 |pages=3952–3967 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-294X.2010.04797.x|pmid=20854275 |s2cid=205363121 }} ''S. inaequidens'' commonly exists in ruderal habitats such as railroads, roads and motorways, vacant or disused land.{{cite journal |last1=Lachmuth |first1=Susanne |last2=Durka |first2=Walter |last3=Schurr |first3=Frank M. |title=Differentiation of reproductive and competitive ability in the invaded range of Senecio inaequidens: the role of genetic Allee effects, adaptive and nonadaptive evolution |journal=New Phytologist |date=October 2011 |volume=192 |issue=2 |pages=529–541 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-8137.2011.03808.x|pmid=21736567 |doi-access=free }}{{cite journal |journal=Acta Musei Silesiae, Scientiae Naturales |volume=65 |issue=2 |pages=129–133 |author=Pietr Kocián | doi=10.1515/cszma-2016-0016|title=The first records of Senecio inaequidens along motorways in Poland and Slovakia|year=2016 |doi-access=free }} Plants can be seen on disused land as [[pioneer species]] but so far often disappear in an [[ecological succession]]. In Central Europe where it first spread, the plant so far seems to use previously unused ecological niches. There does not seem a clear advantage over native vegetation, except in higher altitude. In the European Alps ecologists and farmers are worried that it has the advantage of invading grazing fields on the [[Alpine transhumance|alm pastures]].{{cite journal |last1=Vacchiano |first1=G. |last2=Barni |first2=E. |last3=Lonati |first3=M. |last4=Masante |first4=D. |last5=Curtaz |first5=A. |last6=Tutino |first6=S. |last7=Siniscalco |first7=C. |title=Monitoring and modeling the invasion of the fast spreading alien ''S. inaequidens'' DC. in an alpine region |journal=Plant Biosystems |date=27 November 2013 |volume=147 |issue=4 |pages=1139–1147 |doi=10.1080/11263504.2013.861535|hdl=2434/564238 |s2cid=55444936 |hdl-access=free }} The furthest north it was found was [[Norway]].{{cite web|url=http://www.fylkesmannen.no/hoved.aspx?m=4770&amid=3453667|title=Boersvineblom funnet på Sjursøya i Oslo|date=19 October 2010|publisher=County Governor's Office in Oslo and Akershus|language=Norwegian| access-date=22 October 2010}} ''S. inaequidens'' is also present in Korea and Taiwan.{{cite journal |title=Two Newly Naturalized Plants in Korea: Senecio inaequidens DC. and S. scandens Buch.-Ham. ex D.Don |journal=Journal of Asia-Pacific Biodiversity |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=449–453 |doi=10.7229/jkn.2013.6.4.00449|year=2013 |last1=Jang |first1=Jin |last2=Park |first2=Su Hyun |last3=Jung |first3=Su Young |last4=Chang |first4=Kae Sun |last5=Yang |first5=Jong Cheol |last6=Oh |first6=Seung Hwan |last7=Han |first7=Yang Soon |last8=Yun |first8=Seok Min |doi-access=free }} In South America and Australia the diploid variant ''[[Senecio madagascariensis|S. madagascariensis]]'' is highly invasive.{{cite journal |last1=LÓPEZ |first1=MARIANA G. |last2=WULFF |first2=ARTURO F. |last3=POGGIO |first3=LIDIA |last4=XIFREDA |first4=CECILIA C. |title=South African fireweed (Asteraceae) in Argentina: relevance of chromosome studies to its systematics |journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society |date=December 2008 |volume=158 |issue=4 |pages=613–620 |doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.2008.00865.x|doi-access=free }} ==Properties== ''Senecio inaequidens'' contains [[pyrrolizidine alkaloids]] having hepatotoxic properties that are poisonous to mammals.{{cite journal |title=The toxicity of Senecio inaequidens DC. |journal=Journal of the South African Veterinary Association |volume=78 |issue=3 |pages=121–9 |doi=10.4102/jsava.v78i3.302|pmid=18237033 |year=2007 |last1=Dimande |first1=A.F.P. |last2=Botha |first2=C.J. |last3=Prozesky
